analysis.one_liner: Makes destroying audit records and defrauding investors federal crimes and protects corporate whistleblowers.
analysis.headline: A response to the Enron-era corporate scandals, the bill drew 35 cosponsors — every one a Democrat or the House's lone independent — and died in a Judiciary subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, introduced months after Enron's collapse, would have made it a federal crime to destroy documents to obstruct an investigation (up to 5 years in prison), to destroy corporate audit records, and to defraud investors in publicly traded securities (up to 10 years). It would also have kept executives from erasing fraud judgments by declaring bankruptcy, doubled the wages bankruptcy protects for laid-off workers, given whistleblowers at public companies a right to sue over retaliation with double back pay, extended the deadline for investors to sue over fraud to five years, and created a Justice Department unit focused on pension and securities fraud. It never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors and retirement savers, who get criminal penalties for securities fraud, longer to sue over fraud, and fraud judgments that cannot be wiped out in bankruptcy; employees of public companies, who gain whistleblower protection with reinstatement and double back pay; and workers whose wages get stronger priority in corporate bankruptcies.

how_it_helps.text: Creates new federal crimes: destroying or falsifying records to obstruct a federal investigation or bankruptcy case, and destroying corporate audit records, each punishable by up to 5 years in prison [S3].
Makes it a stand-alone federal crime to run a scheme to defraud investors in publicly traded securities, punishable by up to 10 years in prison [S3].
Makes debts from securities-fraud judgments or settlements non-dischargeable in bankruptcy, so executives cannot erase fraud judgments by filing Chapter 11 [S3].
Increases bankruptcy wage protection for employees from $4,000 to $10,000 and from 90 to 180 days of unpaid wages [S3].

Gives employees of public companies who report fraud a private right to sue over retaliation, with reinstatement, double back pay, and attorney fees, and bars companies from forcing these claims into arbitration [S3].
Extends the deadline for private securities-fraud lawsuits to the earlier of five years after the violation or three years after discovery [S3].
Directs the Justice Department to create a Retirement Security Fraud Bureau to detect and prosecute pension and securities fraud [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded companies and their executives face new criminal exposure, longer liability windows, and bankruptcy-proof fraud judgments; accounting firms must retain audit documents for five years under penalty of prison; companies bear whistleblower lawsuits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Public companies, their executives, and audit firms

drawbacks.text: The whistleblower claim must be filed within 180 days of the retaliation, a short window for an employee deciding whether to challenge an employer [S3].
Whistleblower remedies include twice the back pay and possible punitive damages, which companies would bear as new litigation costs and risk [S3].
The five-year document-retention mandate for auditors is backed by criminal penalties, which good-faith critics could see as a blunt tool for routine record-management decisions.
The bill raises criminal penalties and extends liability without any offsetting relief for companies, adding compliance and litigation costs that could be passed to shareholders and customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to the people hurt hardest by corporate fraud — retirement savers, investors, and employees of collapsing companies — and the costs fall on the executives, auditors, and public companies in a position to commit the fraud. The strongest honest objection is design, not direction: the 180-day whistleblower deadline is short and the criminal document rules are broad, but on the core question the bill aims penalties at the people with power over the money. In practice this exact bill never became law, but months later the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 enacted nearly identical provisions on document destruction, audit record retention, whistleblower protection, and the securities-fraud statute of limitations — so the public largely got these protections anyway through different legislation.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee, which sent it to its Crime subcommittee, and nothing further ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 9, 2002 by Rep. John Conyers with 20 original cosponsors including House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt, Reps. Barney Frank, John Dingell, and John LaFalce [S3].
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
On May 6, 2002 it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, its last recorded action [S5].
It finished with 35 cosponsors — 34 of the chamber's 208 House Democrats plus the chamber's one independent — and no Republican cosponsors [S4].
The bill never received a subcommittee or committee vote and never reached the House floor [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In the immediate term, public companies, their executives, and audit firms were better off with the bill dead, avoiding new criminal exposure and liability. But the loss to investors was largely offset months later when Congress passed the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 (well outside the provided record, but widely known) with nearly identical document-destruction, whistleblower, and statute-of-limitations provisions — meaning the main difference this bill's death made was timing, not substance.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public companies and audit firms, briefly

for.name: Rep. John Conyers
for.role: Sponsor; Ranking Member, House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured 34 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents

against.name: Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled it for a committee markup or floor action; it was instead routed to a subcommittee and stayed there

sides.party_line_note: All 35 cosponsors were House Democrats or the chamber's single independent, no Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired Judiciary Committee took no action on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Publicly traded companies and their executives
industries.note: The bill adds criminal penalties for securities fraud and record destruction, extends the window for investor lawsuits to five years, and makes fraud judgments survive bankruptcy. Its provisions apply specifically to issuers of publicly traded securities.

Auditors of public companies would have to keep all audit documents for five years, with prison time for willful destruction. This targets the firms whose clean audits helped conceal frauds like Enron's.

industries.industry: Insurers and employers facing whistleblower claims
industries.note: Public companies could no longer force whistleblower retaliation claims into arbitration and would face double-back-pay damages. The provision shifts leverage to employees who report fraud.
